# Kribble: full blog text

Kribble is a childcare discovery and booking app for parents in India, launching first in Gurugram (Gurgaon). Its team physically visits and checks every daycare, preschool and playschool before listing it. Parents will be able to compare fees, plans and facilities, book anything from a single day (One-Day Daycare) to a full year, pay in the app and get daily updates from the centre. Kribble is pre-launch; parents can join the waitlist at kribblecare.com.


---

# 12 daycare red flags parents should never ignore
URL: https://www.kribblecare.com/blog/daycare-red-flags/

The biggest daycare red flags are hidden rooms, staff who ignore or snap at children, and vague answers about safety, pickup or fees. After enrolment, watch for unexplained injuries, sudden changes in your child, and a centre that gets defensive when you ask questions.

One red flag doesn't always mean a bad centre. But each one deserves a clear answer before you trust them with your child.

## Red flags on a visit

### 1. You can't see the rooms where children spend the day

A good centre shows you the classrooms, nap room, toilets and kitchen. It might ask you to keep quiet during naps, which is fair.

If you are kept in the office or reception, or told you can only visit by appointment outside working hours, ask why. Openness is a basic sign of a centre with nothing to hide.

### 2. Staff ignore crying children or speak harshly

Watch how caregivers respond when a child is upset. A warm centre comforts quickly and calmly.

Shouting, sarcasm, threats or leaving a child to cry alone for long periods are all reasons to walk away.

### 3. Too many children for the adults in the room

Count the adults and children yourself. If one adult is clearly stretched across a large group of toddlers, attention and safety suffer.

Our teacher-to-child ratio guide explains what is reasonable for each age.

### 4. Anyone can walk in

Notice how you got in. An unlocked gate, no sign-in and no one asking who you are suggests the same is true at pickup time.

### 5. Vague answers about who can collect a child

Ask what happens if someone other than you turns up at pickup. A good answer is specific: a written authorisation list, photo ID and a call to you.

"We know all the parents" is not a policy.

### 6. Dirty toilets, kitchen or nappy area

Young children put everything in their mouths. Look at the places that are hardest to keep clean: toilets, changing areas, the kitchen and the floor where babies crawl.

A strong smell, overflowing bins or no hand-washing after nappy changes are clear warning signs.

### 7. Obvious safety hazards

Look for uncovered sockets, unguarded stairs or balconies, open windows, loose wires, and cleaning products or medicines within reach. These are simple to fix. A centre that hasn't fixed them may not be paying attention.

Our [daycare safety checklist](/blog/daycare-safety-checklist/) has 20 things to check.

### 8. No staff checks

Ask whether every staff member, including helpers, drivers and cleaners, has been background or police verified. Hesitation, or "only the teachers", is a red flag.

### 9. Pressure to pay on the spot

Be cautious of "only one seat left, pay the admission fee today" or a large non-refundable deposit before you've had time to think. A good centre gives you fees in writing and time to decide.

Our guide to [daycare fees](/blog/daycare-fees-explained/) explains what's normal and what to ask about refunds.

## Red flags after enrolment

### 10. Incidents you hear about late, or not at all

Small bumps and scrapes happen with young children. What matters is that you're told the same day, with a short explanation.

If you find bruises or marks that no one mentions, or the explanation changes, ask for a meeting.

### 11. Defensive or evasive answers

You should be able to ask questions and get calm, direct replies. If staff become irritated, change the subject or tell you to "just trust us", take note.

The same goes for a centre that discourages you from dropping in or calling during the day.

### 12. A lasting change in your child

Some tears at drop-off are normal, especially in the first few weeks. Our guide to settling into daycare explains what usually happens.

Pay attention if your child becomes fearful of a particular person, refuses to go after settling well, or shows other changes that last. You know your child best. If something feels wrong, trust that feeling and look into it.

## What to do if you spot a red flag

**Before you enrol:** ask about it directly. Sometimes there is a good explanation. If there isn't, or the answer doesn't reassure you, move on. There are other centres.

**After you enrol:**

1. Write down what you saw or heard, with dates and times.
2. Ask for a meeting with the centre head, not just a word at pickup.
3. Ask for specifics: what happened, who was there and what has changed since.
4. If the answer doesn't satisfy you, consider moving your child.
5. If you believe your child has been harmed, contact the police and seek medical care for your child. Your child's safety comes before any fee or contract.

Talk to other parents at the centre if you feel comfortable. You may not be the only one who has noticed.

## Use red flags as part of a bigger picture

Red flags are the "no" list. You also need a "yes" list: warm staff, a sensible routine, clean spaces and good communication. Our [complete guide to choosing a daycare](/blog/how-to-choose-a-daycare/) covers both, and our [questions to ask on a visit](/blog/questions-to-ask-daycare-visit/) help you test each area.

Kribble's team visits and checks every centre before it is listed, but that is not a guarantee. Your own visit and instincts still matter most.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is it a red flag if a daycare doesn't allow surprise visits?

Not always. Some centres limit drop-ins during naps or settling-in times to avoid upsetting children. But a centre should welcome you at some point during a normal day, and should never keep you away entirely.

### What should I do if my child comes home with an unexplained injury?

Ask the centre that day for an explanation and for their incident record. Young children do get small bumps, but staff should already have told you. If the answer is unclear or keeps changing, ask for a meeting with the centre head.

### Is crying at drop-off a sign of a bad daycare?

Usually not. Many children cry at drop-off for the first few weeks and settle soon after you leave. Ask staff how long the crying lasts. A lasting change in your child, or fear of a specific person, deserves a closer look.

### Should I leave a daycare after one bad experience?

It depends on how the centre responds. A centre that explains what happened, owns any mistake and tells you what it has changed may deserve another chance. One that gets defensive or vague is harder to trust.

# Daycare and preschool fees explained: admission, monthly, annual and hidden costs
URL: https://www.kribblecare.com/blog/daycare-fees-explained/

Daycare and preschool fees in India usually have three layers: one-time charges at admission, a regular fee (monthly, quarterly or annual), and extras such as meals, transport and activities. The headline monthly fee rarely tells you the full cost. Ask for every charge in writing before you pay anything.

Here is what each fee means, what to ask about it, and how to compare centres fairly.

## One-time fees

These are paid when you enrol. They can add up to a large sum before your child's first day.

### Registration or application fee

A small fee to process your application or hold an assessment visit. It is usually non-refundable.

**Ask:** Is this adjusted against the admission fee if we join?

### Admission fee

A one-time fee to confirm your child's place. At premium centres it can be substantial. For example, one premium chain's one-time admission fee is listed at about ₹28,000 on [Kiddenz](https://kiddenz.com/brand/klay).

**Ask:** Is any of it refundable if we withdraw before the start date? Does it cover only this year, or the whole time my child is at the centre?

### Security deposit (caution money)

A refundable amount held against damage or unpaid fees.

**Ask:** When is it refunded, how, and what can be deducted? Get the answer in writing.

## Regular fees

### Monthly, quarterly, half-yearly or annual plans

Most centres let you pay at different intervals. Paying for a longer period upfront sometimes earns a discount. It also means more money at stake if you leave early.

**Ask:** What is the total yearly cost on each plan? What happens to advance fees if we leave mid-term?

### Half-day vs full-day

Daycares often charge differently for half-day and full-day care. A preschool plus afternoon daycare may be billed as two separate fees.

**Ask:** If my child does preschool in the morning and daycare after, what is the combined monthly cost?

## Extras and hidden costs

These are the charges parents most often miss. Some centres include them; others bill separately.

| Extra | What to check |
|---|---|
| Meals and snacks | Included, or a separate monthly charge? |
| Transport | Cost by distance? Is there a female attendant on the van? |
| Extended hours | Cost per hour, or a flat late fee? |
| Annual or activity charges | Books, stationery, uniforms, events, field trips |
| Summer and holiday care | Included in the plan, or charged as a camp? |
| Nappies, wipes and bedding | Do you supply them, or are they charged? |
| Fee increases | How much did fees rise last year? When is the next increase? |

Late pickup fees deserve a close look if your work hours are unpredictable. A few late evenings a month can add up quickly.

## Refunds, notice and withdrawal

This is where misunderstandings happen. Ask these before you pay:

- How much notice must we give to withdraw?
- If we pay quarterly or annually, are unused months refunded?
- Is the security deposit returned in full, and how soon?
- What happens if the centre closes, moves or changes timings?
- Are fees charged during long absences, such as illness or travel?

Get the answers in writing, ideally in the fee receipt or admission form. A good centre is happy to put its policies on paper.

## What a typical fee range looks like

Fees vary widely by city, area and type of centre. As one example, Gurgaon listings on [Kiddenz](https://kiddenz.com/gurugram) show a median of about ₹55,400 a year. The range runs from about ₹16,000 to ₹2 lakh a year.

Our guide to [preschool and daycare fees in Gurgaon](/blog/preschool-fees-gurgaon/) goes area by area. If you live in Gurgaon, the [Gurgaon daycare guide](/blog/daycare-in-gurgaon-guide/) covers fee bands alongside other things to check.

## What drives the price

Higher fees often reflect location, rent, building size, brand and facilities. They don't always mean better care.

What usually matters more for your child: stable, trained staff, a good ratio of adults to children, and a centre that communicates well. A modest centre that gets these right can be better value than a premium one that doesn't.

## How to compare fees fairly

Comparing monthly fees alone can mislead you. One centre's lower fee may exclude meals and transport. Another's higher fee may include everything.

To compare properly:

1. Ask each centre for its full fee sheet in writing.
2. Add every one-time and recurring charge to get a first-year total.
3. Note what is included: meals, hours, holidays, materials.
4. Compare refund and notice terms, not just prices.
5. Put it all in one table. Our daycare comparison scorecard gives you a template.

Fees are one part of the decision. Our [complete daycare checklist](/blog/how-to-choose-a-daycare/) covers the rest, from safety to staff.

When Kribble launches, you'll be able to see admission, monthly, quarterly and annual plans side by side. You'll also be able to pay fees in the app, with receipts and reminders.

## Frequently asked questions

### Are daycare admission fees refundable?

Usually not, though it depends on the centre. Some refund part of it if you withdraw before the start date. Always ask, and get the answer in writing before you pay.

### Is it better to pay daycare fees monthly or annually?

Annual payment sometimes comes with a discount, but you have more money at risk if you leave early. Monthly payment costs more over time but gives you flexibility. If you're unsure about a centre, start monthly.

### What is a security deposit at a daycare?

It is a refundable amount the centre holds against unpaid fees or damage. Ask when and how it is returned, and what can be deducted, before you pay.

### Why do daycare fees vary so much?

Location, rent, building, brand and facilities all affect price. Staff quality and ratios matter more for your child, and they don't always track the fee. Compare what is included, not just the headline number.

# What does a "verified" daycare actually mean?
URL: https://www.kribblecare.com/blog/what-verified-daycare-means/

A "verified" daycare usually means someone has checked that the centre exists and matches what it claims. What that check covers depends entirely on who did it and how. It is not a government licence, and it is never a guarantee that your child will be safe.

The word "verified" is everywhere now. On listing sites, on Google, on Instagram. So it's worth knowing what to ask when you see it.

## Three very different kinds of "verified"

| Type | What usually happens | What it tells you |
|---|---|---|
| Phone or email check | Someone confirms the centre's contact details | The centre exists and answers the phone |
| Document check | The centre uploads papers like registration or a fire certificate | Some paperwork exists, as of the upload date |
| In-person visit | Someone goes to the centre and looks around | The place matches its photos and claims, on that day |

These are not the same. A badge from a phone call and a badge from a site visit can look identical on a screen. Always ask, "Verified how, and when?"

## What a visit can check

A physical visit is the strongest of the three. A trained visitor can see things that never show up in photos:

- Whether the address, rooms and facilities match the listing
- Whether the space looks clean and child-proofed
- Whether there are working basics, such as a secure entrance and a first aid kit
- How many adults and children are actually present
- Whether fees and timings match what's advertised

That's real, useful information. It saves you from wasted trips to centres that look nothing like their photos.

## What a visit can't check

Even a careful visit is a snapshot. It cannot tell you:

- **How the centre runs on other days.** A visit sees one morning. Staffing and mood can change week to week.
- **Every adult's history.** A visitor can ask whether staff are police verified. They usually can't confirm every record themselves.
- **How staff behave when no one is watching.** No outside check can fully answer this.
- **Whether your child will be happy there.** That depends on your child, and only time shows it.

This is why verification helps you shortlist, not decide.

## Verification is not a licence

In India, rules for registering preschools and daycares vary by state and type of centre. A listing site's "verified" badge is not the same as government registration. It doesn't replace it, and it doesn't prove it.

If registration matters to you, ask the centre directly what it is registered as, and with whom. A good centre will answer plainly.

## What you should still check yourself

Use verification to narrow your list. Then do your own homework on the two or three centres left:

1. **Visit in person, twice if you can.** Once at drop-off, once mid-morning. Our [questions to ask on a daycare visit](/blog/questions-to-ask-daycare-visit/) will help.
2. **Run the safety basics.** Go through the [daycare safety checklist](/blog/daycare-safety-checklist/): staff checks, pickup rules, first aid, fire exits, hygiene.
3. **Ask about policies in writing.** Child protection, sick children, incidents, fees and refunds.
4. **Talk to current parents.** Ask the centre to connect you, or chat at the gate at pickup time.
5. **Try a day.** A trial day shows you how your child responds and how staff handle the real thing.
6. **Watch for red flags.** Keep our list of [daycare red flags](/blog/daycare-red-flags/) in mind, before and after you enrol.

For the full process, see [how to choose a daycare](/blog/how-to-choose-a-daycare/).

## Good questions to ask any "verified" platform

- Who did the verification, and were they trained?
- Was it an in-person visit, a call or a document upload?
- When was the centre last checked?
- What happens if a parent reports a problem?
- Can a centre pay to be verified, or to rank higher?

Clear answers are a good sign. Vague ones mean the badge is mostly decoration.

## How we approach it

Every centre listed on Kribble will have been physically visited and checked by our team before it appears in the app. That means a real person has been there. It does not mean a government licence or a safety guarantee, and you should still visit yourself. You can read more about [what we're building](/blog/what-is-kribble/).

## Frequently asked questions

### What does "verified daycare" mean?

It means someone has checked the centre against some standard, but the standard varies a lot. It could be a phone call, a document upload or an in-person visit. Always ask who verified it, how and when.

### Is a verified daycare guaranteed to be safe?

No. Verification is a snapshot of what someone saw or checked at one point. It helps you shortlist, but you should still visit, ask questions and try a day before you enrol.

### Is verification the same as a government licence?

No. A listing site's badge is separate from any government registration. Rules for registering daycares and preschools vary by state, so ask the centre directly what it is registered as.

### What should I check myself even if a daycare is verified?

Visit in person, go through a safety checklist, ask for key policies in writing and talk to current parents. A trial day is one of the best ways to see how the centre really works.

# Your nanny cancelled: backup childcare options for working parents
URL: https://www.kribblecare.com/blog/backup-childcare-one-day/

When your nanny cancels, your backup childcare options are family or neighbours, an office creche, a single day at a daycare, or splitting the day. The families who cope best set these up in advance.

Every working parent hits this: a nanny's family wedding, a festival closure, an unwell grandparent. Here's how to be ready.

## Your backup options, compared

| Option | Best for | Set up in advance | Watch out for |
|---|---|---|---|
| Grandparents or family | Short notice, sick children | Agree when they're available | Distance, their own health and plans |
| Trusted neighbour or friend | A few hours, school-age children | Swap favours, share contacts | Not a long-term fix |
| Another parent in your child's class | Older toddlers and preschoolers | Exchange numbers, offer to return the favour | Both families may need help on the same day |
| Office creche or tie-up | Weekdays, if your employer has one | Register early, check age limits | Seats can be limited |
| One-day or hourly daycare | A full workday | Find and check a centre before you need it | Your child won't know the place |
| Parents split the day | Half days, flexible jobs | Agree the rota in advance | Hard on long meeting days |
| Work from home | Older children, light workdays | Know your manager's stance | Very hard with a baby or toddler |

Most families use two or three of these. Pick a first choice and a second, so you're not starting from zero.

## Option 1: Family, friends and neighbours

This is often the most comforting backup for a child. It works best when it's agreed, not assumed.

- Ask now, not on the day: "If our nanny is off, could you help on weekdays?"
- Keep a small kit at their home: spare clothes, nappies, a favourite toy.
- Share your child's routine, allergies and your paediatrician's number in writing.

If you rely on another parent, offer to return the favour. Shared backups last longer.

## Option 2: Your office creche

If you work for a larger employer, you may have access to a creche or a tie-up with a nearby centre. In India, establishments with 50 or more employees are [required to provide one](https://www.pib.gov.in/FactsheetDetails.aspx?id=150473), either their own or a shared creche. Our guide to creches at work in India explains the rules and how to ask HR.

Register early, even if you only plan to use it as backup. Check age limits, timings and how much notice they need.

## Option 3: One-day daycare

Some daycares take children for a single day or a few hours. It can be the most practical option when nobody else is free and you have a full workday.

Because your child won't know the place, prepare:

1. **Find the centre in advance.** Don't search on the morning you need it.
2. **Visit once, ideally with your child.** Use our [questions to ask on a visit](/blog/questions-to-ask-daycare-visit/), at least the safety ones.
3. **Check the basics.** Staff checks, pickup rules and first aid. Our [daycare safety checklist](/blog/daycare-safety-checklist/) helps.
4. **Pack familiar things.** A comfort toy, a known snack and a note on naps and food.
5. **Share your details clearly.** Allergies, emergency contacts and who will collect.

A single day can also double as a trial. If you're choosing a regular centre, see why you should try a daycare for a day.

## Option 4: Share it between parents

Sometimes the best backup is the two of you: one takes the morning, the other the afternoon. Our guide to dads and daycare has practical ideas for sharing it fairly.

## How to prepare, in one evening

Set aside an hour this week and do these:

1. **Write your backup list.** First choice, second choice, and their numbers.
2. **Check your leave.** Know how many days you and your partner can take, and how fast.
3. **Find one centre that takes single days.** Visit it before you need it.
4. **Make a one-page child info sheet.** Routine, food, allergies, medicines, doctor's number, emergency contacts.
5. **Pack a backup bag.** Clothes, nappies or spare underwear, a snack box and a comfort toy.
6. **Tell your manager your plan.** It's easier to ask for flexibility before a crisis.

## When your nanny cancels often

If backup has become weekly, the main plan may need a rethink. Talk to your nanny about what's going on. Consider whether a daycare, or a mix of nanny and daycare, would suit you better. Our guide on [how to choose a daycare](/blog/how-to-choose-a-daycare/) walks you through it, and [preschool vs daycare](/blog/preschool-vs-daycare/) helps if your child is older.

Kribble will offer One-Day Daycare, so you'll be able to book a single day at a verified centre in Gurugram. On-demand caregivers at home are part of the plan too.

## Frequently asked questions

### What can I do if my nanny cancels at the last minute?

Call your first backup: a family member, neighbour or another parent. If no one is free, check your office creche or a daycare that takes single days. Splitting the day between parents can also work.

### Can I send my child to a daycare for just one day?

Some daycares do take children for a single day or a few hours. Find and visit one in advance, so you've checked safety basics before you need it. Pack familiar things to help your child settle.

### How do I prepare backup childcare in advance?

Write a list of first and second choices. Find one centre that takes single days. Make a one-page sheet on your child's routine and allergies, and keep a bag packed.

### Is one-day daycare safe for a toddler who has never been there?

It can work well with preparation, but it depends on the centre and your child. Visit together first, check the safety basics and pack comfort items. A centre's team should welcome your questions.

# Why toddlers can't "just calm down", and what actually helps
URL: https://www.kribblecare.com/blog/toddler-meltdowns-what-helps/

Toddler meltdowns happen because a young child's ability to manage big feelings is still being built. They are not being naughty, and they cannot "just calm down" on command. What helps most is a calm adult nearby who lends them some of that calm until the storm passes.

## Why a toddler can't switch the feeling off

Think of self-control as a skill, like walking or talking. Toddlers are still learning it.

The parts of the brain that help us pause, think and choose a response keep developing through early childhood and well beyond. A two-year-old feels frustration, hunger or disappointment at full volume. The brakes are not fully fitted yet.

When the banana breaks, your child isn't being dramatic. To them, it is a real loss they can't yet put in perspective.

### Common triggers

Most meltdowns have a simple cause underneath. Look for these first:

- **Tiredness**: a missed nap or a late night.
- **Hunger**: a long gap between meals.
- **Transitions**: leaving the park, switching off a toy, getting into the car seat.
- **Not being understood**: they know what they want but can't say it.
- **Too much**: noise, crowds, a busy day of new faces.
- **Big changes**: a new sibling, a move, or starting daycare.

Spot a pattern and you can often prevent the next one.

## Co-regulation: lending your calm

Children learn to calm themselves by being calmed by someone else, many times over. This is called co-regulation.

When you stay steady, your voice, face and breathing send a signal: "This is big, but we're okay." Over months and years, your child starts to do this for themselves.

It does not mean giving in. You can hold the limit ("We're not buying the toy") and stay kind at the same time.

## Three steps that help in the moment

### 1. Get down to eye level

Kneel or sit so you are at their height. Standing over a crying child can feel like a threat, even when you mean well.

Keep your voice low and slow, and use few words.

### 2. Name the feeling

Say what you see, simply. "You're angry. You wanted to stay at the park."

Naming the feeling tells your child you understand. Over time it also gives them the words to say it instead of screaming it.

Avoid "Stop crying" or "It's nothing". To them, it is not nothing.

### 3. Wait

This is the hard part. Stay close and let the feeling run its course.

You don't have to fix it or talk them out of it. If they want a hug, offer one. If they push you away, stay nearby and say, "I'm right here."

Once they are calm, talk briefly about what happened or simply move on.

### What not to expect

| What you might hope for | What is realistic for a toddler |
|---|---|
| They calm down when told to | They calm down when helped |
| They explain why they were upset | They may not know or have the words |
| Meltdowns stop after a few weeks | They become shorter and less frequent over time |
| A good routine prevents all of them | It prevents many, not all |

## Meltdowns at daycare

Many parents worry when they hear about a meltdown at daycare. It is common, especially in the first weeks. If your child is new, our guide to settling into daycare covers what is normal.

What matters is how the staff respond. You want carers who stay calm, comfort the child and keep them safe, rather than shaming or isolating them.

### What to ask a daycare

Add these to your list of [questions to ask on a visit](/blog/questions-to-ask-daycare-visit/):

- "What do you do when a child is very upset?" A good answer sounds like: "One of us stays with them, gets down to their level and helps them calm down."
- "Do you use time-outs?" Listen for whether the child is left alone. Staying close is better at this age.
- "How do you tell parents about a hard day?" Look for honest, specific updates, not just "fine".
- "How do you handle a child who bites or hits during a meltdown?" You want a calm plan: separate, comfort both children, tell both families.

The way a centre handles big feelings tells you a lot about its care overall. It belongs on your [daycare checklist](/blog/how-to-choose-a-daycare/) alongside safety and hygiene.

It also helps to know what daily updates to expect from your daycare.

## When to talk to someone

Most toddler meltdowns are a normal part of growing up. If you are worried about how often they happen, how long they last, or anything else about your child's development, speak to your paediatrician. They know your child and can guide you.

When Kribble launches, you'll be able to see a centre's approach before you visit and get notes from your child's teachers in one feed.

## Frequently asked questions

### Why do toddlers have so many meltdowns?

Toddlers feel strong emotions but are still developing the ability to manage them. Tiredness, hunger, transitions and not being understood are common triggers. Meltdowns usually become shorter and less frequent as language and self-control grow.

### Should I ignore a toddler's tantrum?

Ignoring the feeling usually doesn't help a toddler calm down. You can hold a limit while staying close and calm. Getting to eye level, naming the feeling and waiting with them tends to work better than walking away.

### Is it normal for my child to have meltdowns at daycare?

Yes, especially in the first few weeks or after a change at home. What matters is that staff respond calmly and comfort your child. Ask the centre how they handle big feelings and how they will let you know.

### How can I prevent toddler meltdowns?

You can't prevent all of them, but you can reduce many. Keep naps and meals regular, warn your child before transitions, and keep busy days short. Spotting your child's own triggers helps most.

# How to choose a daycare: the complete checklist for Indian parents
URL: https://www.kribblecare.com/blog/how-to-choose-a-daycare/

To choose a daycare, shortlist three or four centres near home or work and visit each on a normal working day. Check safety, staff, ratios, hygiene, food, communication and fees. Then try your top choice for a day before you pay anything large. Your own gut feel, after a proper look, counts for more than any brochure.

Below is each step, with what to look at and what to ask. There is a printable checklist at the end.

## Step 1: Decide what kind of care you need

Before you visit anywhere, get clear on three things. How old is your child? What hours do you need? And do you need care, early learning, or both?

A daycare covers long working hours, with meals and naps. A preschool or playschool runs shorter hours and focuses on early learning. Many centres combine both. Our guide to [preschool vs daycare vs playschool](/blog/preschool-vs-daycare/) explains the differences and which suits which age.

Write down your must-haves before you start:

- Opening and closing times, including how late you could realistically arrive
- Days you need (weekdays only, or Saturdays too)
- Maximum distance or travel time from home or office
- Your monthly budget, including one-time fees
- Any dietary needs or allergies

## Step 2: Build a shortlist

Start with centres within a commute you can manage twice a day, every day. A centre that is excellent but 50 minutes away in traffic will wear you down.

Ask other parents in your building or office. Treat online reviews as a starting point, not a verdict.

Call each centre with three quick questions. Is there a place for your child's age? What are the hours? What is the total monthly fee?

Drop any centre that can't give a straight answer on fees. Clear answers early usually mean clear communication later.

## Step 3: Visit on a normal working day

Book your visit for mid-morning on a weekday, when children are there and the routine is running. An empty centre on a Saturday tells you very little.

Stay at least 30 to 45 minutes. Watch more than you listen. Bring our list of [25 questions to ask on a daycare visit](/blog/questions-to-ask-daycare-visit/) so you don't forget anything.

### Safety and security

Notice how you get in. Was the gate or door locked? Did someone check who you were before letting you through?

Look for:

- A single, controlled entry point
- Covered sockets, guarded stairs and no sharp furniture edges at child height
- Windows and balconies secured
- Cleaning products and medicines locked away
- Fire extinguishers and a clear exit route
- A written list of who is allowed to pick up each child

Ask how they check that the person collecting a child is authorised. A good answer is specific. A list you fill in, photo ID for anyone new, and a call to you if a stranger turns up. For the full list, see our [daycare safety checklist](/blog/daycare-safety-checklist/).

### Staff and caregivers

The people matter more than the building. Watch how caregivers talk to children. Do they kneel to eye level? Do they sound calm and warm, or rushed and sharp?

Ask:

- How long has the lead teacher or caregiver been here?
- What training do staff have in early childhood and first aid?
- Are all staff, including helpers, drivers and cleaners, background or police verified?
- How many staff have left in the past year?

High staff turnover is worth noticing. Young children need familiar faces.

### Ratios and group size

The ratio is the number of children each adult looks after. Fewer children per adult means more attention, especially for babies and toddlers.

India's National ECCE Policy 2013 sets one adult per 20 children aged 3 to 6, and one per 10 under 3 ([summary on Factly](https://factly.in/quality-standards-place-play-schools-pre-schools)). Many parents look for better than this for infants. Count the adults and children in the room yourself. Our teacher-to-child ratio guide explains what is good at each age.

### Hygiene and health

Look at the toilets, the nappy-changing area and the kitchen. Ask to see where children sleep.

Good signs: staff wash hands after nappy changes, toys look clean, and each child has their own bedding. Ask what happens when a child falls ill during the day. A clear sick policy (when to keep a child home, when they call you) protects your child and everyone else's.

### Food and naps

Ask for a sample weekly menu. Is the food cooked on site or brought in? Can they handle allergies or a vegetarian or Jain diet?

For naps, ask where children sleep, who stays with them and how they handle a child who won't settle. A good centre adjusts to your child's routine, especially for under-twos.

### Daily routine and learning

Ask to see the daily schedule. Look for a balance of free play, outdoor time, stories, music, meals and rest.

Be wary of worksheets and rote drills for toddlers. Young children learn best through play and talk.

### Communication with parents

Ask how they will tell you about your child's day. Will you get updates on meals, naps and mood? How are incidents, such as a bump or a bite, reported?

A good centre tells you about every incident the same day, even small ones. Ask whether you can call during the day, and who you would speak to.

## Step 4: Understand the fees in full

The monthly fee is rarely the whole cost. Ask for every charge in writing:

| Fee | What to ask |
|---|---|
| Admission or registration | Is it one-time? Is any part refundable? |
| Security deposit | When and how is it returned? |
| Monthly or term fee | Monthly, quarterly or annual? Any discount for paying ahead? |
| Meals | Included, or extra? |
| Extended hours | What does late pickup cost? |
| Transport | Is it optional? Who is in the van? |
| Activities and materials | Annual charges for books, uniforms, events? |

Ask about notice periods and refunds if you withdraw. Our guide to [daycare and preschool fees](/blog/daycare-fees-explained/) covers each component and hidden costs.

## Step 5: Watch for red flags

Some things should make you pause, however good the rest looks. A centre that won't let you see the rooms where children spend their day. Staff who seem stressed or ignore crying children. Vague answers about who can pick up. Pressure to pay a large deposit on the spot.

Read our list of [12 daycare red flags](/blog/daycare-red-flags/) before your visits so you know what to watch for.

## Step 6: Try a day before you commit

A visit shows you a centre. A trial day shows you how your child responds to it. Ask if you can book a single day, or a few hours, before paying admission fees.

Watch how staff greet your child, how they handle tears and what your child says at pickup. Our guide to trying a daycare for a day explains what to look for.

## Step 7: Compare, then trust your gut

After your visits, compare centres on the same criteria. A simple scoring table helps you see past the nicest reception area. Try our side-by-side daycare scorecard.

Then listen to your instinct. If something felt off and you can't name it, that still counts. If you live in Gurgaon, our [Gurgaon daycare guide](/blog/daycare-in-gurgaon-guide/) covers areas, fee bands and commute planning.

## Printable daycare checklist

Copy this list and take it on every visit.

**Basics**

- Hours, days and commute work for you
- Place available for your child's age

**Safety**

- Locked, controlled entry
- Written pickup authorisation list
- Childproofed rooms, stairs and windows
- First aid and fire safety in place

**Staff**

- Warm, calm caregivers who get down to children's level
- Staff training in early childhood and first aid
- Background or police verification for all staff
- Low staff turnover

**Ratios**

- Adults counted in the room match what you were told
- Smaller groups for babies and toddlers

**Hygiene and food**

- Clean toilets, changing area and kitchen
- Hand-washing after nappy changes and before meals
- Clear sick-child policy
- Sample menu that suits your child

**Communication**

- Daily updates on meals, naps and mood
- Same-day incident reporting
- Easy to reach someone during the day

**Fees**

- Every charge listed in writing
- Clear refund and notice terms
- No pressure to pay on the spot

**Gut feel**

- Your child seemed comfortable
- You felt welcome to ask questions

## A shortcut for your shortlist

Kribble's team physically visits and checks every centre before it is listed. In the app, you'll be able to compare fees, plans and safety details side by side, starting in Gurugram. Verification is not a guarantee, so a visit is still your best tool.

## Frequently asked questions

### How many daycares should I visit before choosing?

Three or four is usually enough to see the range. Fewer than that and you have nothing to compare against. More than five and the visits start to blur together.

### What is the most important thing to check in a daycare?

The caregivers. Warm, trained, consistent staff who are not stretched across too many children matter more than facilities or decor. Watch how they speak to children when they think no one is looking.

### When should I start looking for a daycare?

Start two to three months before you need care. Popular centres can fill up, and you will want time for visits, a trial day and a settling-in period. If you are returning from maternity leave, start earlier.

### Should I choose a daycare near home or near work?

It depends on who does pickup and how reliable your commute is. Near home suits families sharing pickups, while near office can mean more time with your child on the way. Think about sick days and who can reach the centre fastest.

### Is a costlier daycare always better?

No. Price often reflects location, building and brand rather than care quality. A modest centre with stable, attentive staff can be a better choice than a premium one with high turnover.

# Preschool vs daycare vs playschool: what's the difference and which does your child need?
URL: https://www.kribblecare.com/blog/preschool-vs-daycare/

A daycare looks after your child for most of the working day, with meals and naps. A preschool or playschool runs for a few hours and focuses on early learning through play. If both parents work full days, you usually need a daycare, or a preschool with an attached daycare.

The labels overlap a lot in India, so it helps to look past the name and ask what the centre actually offers.

## The short version

| | Daycare | Preschool | Playschool |
|---|---|---|---|
| Main purpose | Care while parents work | Early learning and school readiness | Play, social skills, first time away from home |
| Typical hours | Long day, often matched to office hours | A few hours, usually mornings | A few hours, usually mornings |
| Typical ages | From infancy, depending on the centre | Roughly 2 to 6 | Roughly 18 months to 3 |
| Meals and naps | Yes | Usually a snack only | Usually a snack only |
| Structure | Routine-based, flexible | Planned activities and themes | Loose, play-led |
| Holidays | Often open most of the year | Follows a school-style calendar | Follows a school-style calendar |

Ages and hours vary by centre, so treat this as a guide and check the details on each visit.

## What a daycare is

A daycare is built around your working day. It covers drop-off before work and pickup after, with meals, naps, nappy changes and play in between.

Many daycares take babies, though the starting age varies. The best ones plan the day carefully, with stories, music, outdoor time and quiet play. Others are closer to supervised care.

Daycares also tend to stay open through school holidays. That matters if your leave is limited.

### What to look for

- Caregivers who stay with the same group of children
- A sensible nap setup, with separate bedding for each child
- Freshly prepared meals and a menu you can see
- Clear updates on meals, sleep and mood each day

## What a preschool is

A preschool focuses on early learning in the years before formal school. Think language, early number sense, motor skills, art, music and getting along with others.

In India, preschool classes often go by names like playgroup, nursery, LKG and UKG. Our guide to the right age for preschool in India explains how these map to your child's age.

Preschool hours are short, usually a morning. That suits families where one parent or a grandparent is home in the afternoon.

### What to look for

- Learning through play, not worksheets for toddlers
- A daily plan that mixes group time, free play and outdoor time
- Teachers trained in early childhood education
- A clear approach, such as Montessori or play-way. Our guide to preschool approaches explains the differences.

## What a playschool is

A playschool is the gentlest start. It is usually for younger children, often a child's first time in a group without a parent.

The focus is play, routine and social skills. Sessions are short, sometimes only a couple of hours.

In practice, many centres use "playschool" and "preschool" for the same thing. Ask what the youngest group does each day, rather than relying on the label.

## Combined centres: preschool plus daycare

Many centres now run a preschool in the morning and a daycare in the afternoon in the same building. Your child attends the preschool classes, then moves to the daycare section until pickup.

This can work very well. Your child stays in one place, with familiar faces, for the whole day.

Ask a few questions first:

- Are the morning teachers and afternoon caregivers different people?
- Is there a proper lunch and nap between the two?
- Does the afternoon have planned activities, or is it mostly waiting for pickup?
- Is the daycare fee separate from the preschool fee?

## How costs compare

Daycare usually costs more per month than preschool, because it covers more hours, meals and staff time. Combined plans are often priced as two parts added together.

Fee structures differ too. Preschools often charge admission plus annual or term fees. Daycares more often bill monthly. Our guide to [daycare and preschool fees](/blog/daycare-fees-explained/) breaks down every component, including the hidden ones.

## Which one does your child need?

Start with your work hours and your child's age. Then use this table.

| Your situation | Child's age | What usually fits |
|---|---|---|
| Both parents work full days | Under 2 | Daycare |
| Both parents work full days | 2 to 6 | Preschool plus daycare, or a full-day daycare with learning built in |
| One parent works part-time or from home | 18 months to 3 | Playschool, a few mornings a week |
| One parent or family member home in afternoons | 2 to 6 | Preschool only |
| Irregular shifts or occasional need | Any | A daycare that offers flexible or single-day plans |
| Preparing for formal school | 3 to 6 | Preschool, with or without daycare |

If your situation sits between two rows, visit both types of centre. Your child's reaction often settles the question.

## Questions to ask whichever you choose

Whatever the label, the basics of good care are the same. Ask about staff training, ratios, safety, pickup rules, sick policy and daily updates. Our [complete daycare checklist](/blog/how-to-choose-a-daycare/) covers each one, and our list of [questions to ask on a visit](/blog/questions-to-ask-daycare-visit/) gives you the exact wording.

When Kribble launches, you'll be able to compare preschool admissions, monthly and half-day daycare and after-school care in one place.

## Frequently asked questions

### Is daycare the same as preschool?

Not quite. Daycare is mainly about care during working hours, while preschool is mainly about early learning for a few hours a day. Many centres offer both under one roof, so the line is often blurred.

### Can my child go to preschool and daycare at the same time?

Yes. Many centres run preschool classes in the morning and daycare in the afternoon. Your child stays in one building all day, which many children find easier than moving between two places.

### Is playschool necessary before preschool?

No. A playschool can help a younger child get used to being in a group, but it is optional. Many children go straight into a preschool class when they are ready.

### Which is better for my child's development, daycare or preschool?

Both can be good. What matters most is warm, trained staff, a sensible ratio and plenty of play. A well-run daycare can offer as much learning as a preschool, and a poor preschool can offer less.


---

# 25 questions to ask on a daycare or preschool visit
URL: https://www.kribblecare.com/blog/questions-to-ask-daycare-visit/

On a daycare or preschool visit, ask about staff, safety, the daily routine, food, sick policy, fees, communication and settling in. The 25 questions below cover all of these. Specific, confident answers are a good sign; vague ones are worth a follow-up.

Print this list or save it on your phone. You won't need every question at every centre, but it helps to have them ready.

## Staff and caregivers

**1. Who will look after my child day to day?**
You want a name, not "our team". Ask to meet them.

**2. What training do your teachers and caregivers have?**
Look for early childhood training and first aid, not only general degrees.

**3. Are all staff police or background verified, including helpers, drivers and cleaners?**
Everyone who is near children matters, not only teachers. A good centre answers yes without hesitation.

**4. How long have your current staff been here?**
Children settle with familiar faces. Frequent changes in staff are worth noticing.

**5. How many children does each adult look after in my child's group?**
Then count during your visit. Our teacher-to-child ratio guide explains what is reasonable at each age.

## Safety and security

**6. How do you control who enters the building?**
Notice whether the gate was locked and whether anyone asked who you were.

**7. Who is allowed to pick up my child, and how do you check?**
A good answer: a written list from you, photo ID for anyone new and a call to you first.

**8. What happens in a medical emergency?**
Ask which hospital is nearest, who takes the child and how quickly you are called.

**9. Do you have CCTV, and who can view it?**
Cameras can help, but they don't replace attentive staff. See our guide to CCTV in daycare.

**10. Do you have a written child protection policy?**
Ask how staff are trained to report concerns and who parents can raise issues with.

## Daily routine and learning

**11. Can I see a typical daily schedule?**
Look for a balance of play, outdoor time, meals, rest and stories.

**12. How much time do children spend outdoors?**
Ask what happens on very hot or polluted days. A good centre has an indoor plan.

**13. How do you approach learning at this age?**
For under-fives, play-based learning is a better sign than worksheets and rote drills.

**14. How do you handle a child who is upset, biting or hitting?**
You want calm, consistent responses. Be wary of any answer that involves shaming or punishment.

## Food and naps

**15. Can I see this week's menu? Is food cooked on site?**
Fresh, simple, balanced meals matter more than a long menu.

**16. How do you manage allergies and dietary needs?**
Ask where allergy information is displayed and how staff are told.

**17. Where and when do children nap, and who stays with them?**
Each child should have their own bedding, and an adult should always be present.

## Health and sickness

**18. When should I keep my child at home?**
A clear sick policy protects your child and everyone else's. Vague rules usually mean illness spreads.

**19. What happens if my child gets ill during the day?**
Ask how quickly you are expected to collect, and where your child waits meanwhile.

**20. Can staff give medicine?**
Ask whether they need written permission and how they record each dose.

## Communication

**21. How will I hear about my child's day?**
Ask whether you get updates on meals, naps, nappies and mood, and how often.

**22. How do you report incidents, even small ones?**
The best answer is "the same day, every time", with a short written note. Our guide to daily updates explains what to expect.

## Fees and policies

**23. What is the full cost, including one-time fees?**
Ask for every charge in writing: admission, deposit, meals, transport, activities and late pickup. See our guide to [daycare fees](/blog/daycare-fees-explained/).

**24. What are the notice and refund terms if we leave?**
Ask how much notice you must give and whether the deposit or any advance fees are refundable.

## Settling in

**25. How do you help a new child settle in?**
A good centre suggests a gradual start, with shorter days in the first week. Ask whether you can stay for part of the first few days. Our guide to settling into daycare has more.

## What a good visit feels like

Answers are only part of it. Watch how staff speak to the children while you are talking to the manager.

Notice whether children seem relaxed and busy, and whether staff answer your questions without getting defensive. If you are told to "just trust us" without detail, ask again.

If anything worries you, compare it against our list of [daycare red flags](/blog/daycare-red-flags/). For the bigger picture of choosing well, read the [complete daycare checklist](/blog/how-to-choose-a-daycare/).

## After the visit

Write down your impressions the same day, before centres blur together. Then, if you can, book a trial day at your top choice.

When Kribble launches, you'll be able to see fees, timings and safety details for centres its team has visited. That means fewer calls before you shortlist.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the most important question to ask a daycare?

Ask who will look after your child each day, and then meet that person. The caregiver your child spends most time with shapes their experience more than any facility.

### How long should a daycare visit take?

Plan for 30 to 45 minutes. That gives you time to ask questions and, more importantly, to watch the children and staff during a normal part of the day.

### Should I take my child on the first visit?

It helps on a second visit or trial day, so you can see how staff respond to your child. On the first visit, going alone lets you focus on asking questions and observing.

### What if the centre won't answer some questions?

Some details, like other families' information, are rightly private. But a centre that avoids questions about safety, staff checks, fees or pickup rules is a centre to think twice about.

# Daycare in Gurgaon: a parent's complete guide for 2026
URL: https://www.kribblecare.com/blog/daycare-in-gurgaon-guide/

Gurgaon has hundreds of daycares and preschools, so the problem is rarely finding one. It's narrowing a long list down to two or three good options near your home or office, at a fee you can sustain. Start with location and hours, then visit, then compare costs in full.

This guide covers how the market looks, what parents pay in different areas, the kinds of centres you'll meet and how to check them.

## How many daycares are there in Gurgaon?

It depends on who is counting. Different directories list different numbers:

- [Kiddenz](https://kiddenz.com/gurugram) lists 567 verified preschools and daycares in Gurgaon.
- [ProEves](https://www.proeves.com/haryana/gurgaon/daycare-in-gurgaon) lists about 429 daycares in Gurgaon.
- We estimate there are about 850 private preschools and daycares across the city, including smaller centres that don't appear on directories.

The numbers differ because each site counts differently, so treat any single figure as a rough guide.

For context, Delhi-NCR is the largest city market for preschool and childcare in India, according to [IMARC](https://www.imarcgroup.com/indian-pre-school-child-care-market). That means lots of choice, and a wide spread in quality and price.

## What does daycare cost in Gurgaon?

Fees vary more than most parents expect. On Kiddenz's Gurgaon listings, the median annual fee is about ₹55,400, with a range from roughly ₹16,000 to ₹2 lakh a year.

Location makes a big difference. Here's what Kiddenz's sector pages show:

| Area | Centres listed on Kiddenz | Median annual fee |
|---|---|---|
| [Sector 51](https://kiddenz.com/gurugram/sector-51) | about 30 | about ₹1.1 lakh |
| Sector 50 | about 29 | not listed here |
| Sector 46 | about 28 | not listed here |
| Sector 45 | about 27 | not listed here |
| Sector 30 | not listed here | about ₹72,800 |
| Sector 92 | not listed here | about ₹32,400 |

So the median in Sector 51 is more than three times that of Sector 92, in the same city.

These are preschool and daycare fees together, and listings change. Treat them as a guide to the range, not a quote. For a full breakdown, read our guide to [preschool and daycare fees in Gurgaon](/blog/preschool-fees-gurgaon/).

### Admission and one-time fees

The yearly fee is only part of the cost. Many centres charge an admission fee, a registration fee or a security deposit on top.

At the premium end, the [Kiddenz page for Klay](https://kiddenz.com/brand/klay) shows annual fees of about ₹1.49 to 1.95 lakh. Admission is a one-time fee of about ₹28,000. At the other end, a franchise preschool in Sector 41 listed on SchoolsUniverse charges about ₹35,000 a year, with about ₹5,000 for admission.

Always ask for the full first-year cost in writing. Our [daycare fees explainer](/blog/daycare-fees-explained/) lists every component to ask about.

## Gurgaon's main areas for daycare

Gurgaon is spread out, and traffic shapes daily life. Here's a quick overview, with a dedicated guide for each area.

### Golf Course Road and DLF Phases 1 to 5

Older, established neighbourhoods close to Cyber City and the main office hubs. Expect a mix of long-running independents and well-known chains. Read our guide to daycare on Golf Course Road and DLF.

### Golf Course Extension and Sohna Road

Newer high-rise societies, many with daycares inside or next to the complex. Read our guide to daycare on Golf Course Extension and Sohna Road.

### Sectors 45 to 51 and South City

One of the densest clusters in the city, with close to 30 centres per sector on Kiddenz. Read our guide to daycare in Sectors 45 to 51.

### Dwarka Expressway and New Gurgaon

Fast-growing areas where many families have moved recently. Many centres are new, and the Sector 92 median fee on Kiddenz is well below the city's. Read our guide to daycare on Dwarka Expressway and New Gurgaon.

## Types of centres you'll find

Most centres in Gurgaon fall into a few types. Each can be excellent or poor. The label tells you little on its own.

| Type | What it usually means | What to check |
|---|---|---|
| National or regional chain | Set curriculum, branded materials, standard policies | Whether this branch follows the policies; how long staff have been here |
| Franchise | Local owner running a brand's programme | Who owns it, how involved they are, how the brand checks quality |
| Independent centre | Owner-run, often in a house or ground floor | Their own safety and pickup policies, in writing |
| Society or in-complex daycare | Inside or next to a residential society | Hours, backup staff, what happens in holidays |
| Workplace creche | Run by or for an employer | Eligibility, waitlist, age range, hours |

Many centres are also combined: a preschool in the morning, daycare in the afternoon. If you're unsure which you need, read [preschool vs daycare vs playschool](/blog/preschool-vs-daycare/).

## Plan around your commute

In Gurgaon, the commute can make or break a good daycare. A great centre an hour away will wear you down within weeks.

Before you visit anywhere, answer these questions:

- **Who does drop-off and pickup on most days?** Choose near that person's route.
- **What happens on a work-from-home day?** A centre near home is easier then.
- **What if your child falls ill at 11 am?** Someone needs to reach the centre fast.
- **What are the centre's hours?** Check the latest pickup time and the late fee.
- **Does the centre offer transport?** Ask who drives, whether there's a female attendant on board, and how many children ride.

Try the route at the real time of day before you commit. Our guide to daycare near home or near office goes through the trade-offs in detail.

## What to check on a visit

The basics are the same anywhere. In Gurgaon, a few points deserve extra attention.

### Safety and access

- Is there one controlled entrance, with someone at it?
- How do they check who collects your child? Ask to see the authorisation form.
- If the centre is in a residential building, how are stairs, balconies and terraces secured?
- Are fire extinguishers visible and in date?

Our [daycare safety checklist](/blog/daycare-safety-checklist/) has the full list.

### Staff and ratio

- How many adults are in your child's room right now? Count them.
- How long have the lead teachers been there?
- Who covers when a teacher is on leave?

See our guide to teacher-to-child ratios for what to look for by age.

### Heat, air and space

Summers are long and hot, and winter air can be poor.

- Where do children play in May and June? Is there a shaded or indoor space?
- How is the indoor play area ventilated and cooled?
- What happens to outdoor play on high-pollution days?

A good answer is specific: "In summer, outdoor time moves to before 9 am. When the air is bad, we play in the activity room."

### Food and routine

- Is food cooked on site, brought in, or sent from home?
- How are allergies handled? Is there a written list in the kitchen?

## Chains vs independents: which is better?

Neither, on its own. A chain gives you predictable policies. An independent may give you a closer relationship with the owner.

What matters is the room your child will be in, the adults in it, and how the centre runs day to day. Judge the branch, not the brand. Use the same [questions on every visit](/blog/questions-to-ask-daycare-visit/) and a simple scorecard to compare fairly.

## A simple plan for Gurgaon parents

1. **Two to three months ahead:** decide on location, hours and budget. Shortlist five or six centres.
2. **Six to eight weeks ahead:** visit at least three. Go at a busy time, not only on a calm tour.
3. **Four weeks ahead:** confirm fees and refund terms in writing. Book a trial day if you can.
4. **Two weeks ahead:** start settling in with short days. See our guide to settling into daycare.

If you want a place for the start of the academic year, ask each centre early how quickly its places fill.

For the full checklist that underpins all of this, read [how to choose a daycare](/blog/how-to-choose-a-daycare/).

Kribble is launching first in Gurugram. Every centre listed will have been visited and checked by the Kribble team. You'll be able to compare fees, timings and real photos side by side.

## Frequently asked questions

### How much is daycare in Gurgaon per month?

It varies widely. Kiddenz's Gurgaon listings show a median annual fee of about ₹55,400, ranging from roughly ₹16,000 to ₹2 lakh a year. Divide the yearly figure by twelve for a rough monthly guide, then add admission, meals and transport.

### Which area of Gurgaon has the most daycares?

On Kiddenz, Sectors 45 to 51 are among the densest, with Sector 51 at about 30 centres and Sector 50 at about 29. That doesn't make it the right area for you. Choose by your commute first.

### Should I choose a daycare near home or near my office?

Near home usually works better if you work from home some days or share pickups. Near office can work if one parent does both trips and has a predictable day. Think about sick days too, since someone will need to reach the centre quickly.

### Are daycares in Gurgaon licensed?

Rules and registration vary, and a listing on any directory is not a licence. Ask each centre what registrations it holds and ask to see them. Then check safety, staff and hygiene yourself on a visit.

# Preschool and daycare fees in Gurgaon: what parents actually pay
URL: https://www.kribblecare.com/blog/preschool-fees-gurgaon/

Preschool fees in Gurgaon range from about ₹16,000 to ₹2 lakh a year, with a median of about ₹55,400, based on [Kiddenz's Gurgaon listings](https://kiddenz.com/gurugram). Where you live changes the number a lot. On top of the yearly fee, expect one-time charges such as admission, which can add thousands more in the first year.

## The citywide picture

Kiddenz lists 567 verified preschools and daycares in Gurgaon (officially Gurugram). Across those listings:

- **Median annual fee:** about ₹55,400
- **Lowest:** roughly ₹16,000 a year
- **Highest:** roughly ₹2 lakh a year

The median means half the listed centres charge less and half charge more. It's a better guide than an average, which a few very expensive centres can pull up.

These figures mix preschools and daycares, and listings change. Use them to set expectations, not to judge a single centre's quote.

## Fees by area

Location is one of the biggest drivers of price. Kiddenz's sector pages show the spread clearly:

| Area | Median annual fee (Kiddenz) |
|---|---|
| [Sector 51](https://kiddenz.com/gurugram/sector-51) | about ₹1.1 lakh |
| Sector 30 | about ₹72,800 |
| Citywide median | about ₹55,400 |
| Sector 92 | about ₹32,400 |

A family in Sector 51 might see a typical fee more than three times higher than a family in Sector 92. Our area guides go into more detail, starting with Sectors 45 to 51 and Dwarka Expressway and New Gurgaon.

## Premium and budget examples

Two real examples show the gap.

At the premium end, the [Kiddenz page for Klay](https://kiddenz.com/brand/klay) shows annual fees of about ₹1.49 to 1.95 lakh. There's a one-time admission fee of about ₹28,000.

At the budget end, a franchise preschool in Sector 41 listed on SchoolsUniverse charges about ₹35,000 a year. Its admission fee is about ₹5,000.

Neither price tells you about quality on its own. A higher fee may pay for longer hours, meals, bigger spaces or a lower ratio. A lower fee may simply reflect lower rent. You only find out by visiting.

## What drives the price

When two centres quote very different fees, it's usually down to a few things:

- **Rent and location.** Space usually costs more on main roads and in high-end sectors.
- **Hours.** A full-day daycare costs more than a three-hour preschool session.
- **Ratio and staffing.** More adults per child means a higher wage bill.
- **Meals.** Cooked meals on site add cost, and some centres charge separately.
- **Space and facilities.** Outdoor play areas, activity rooms and air-conditioning all cost money.
- **Brand.** Chains and franchises may charge for their curriculum and materials.

Ask each centre what the fee covers. A good answer lists it plainly: "Fees include snacks and lunch, materials and the daily updates. Transport and after-hours care are extra."

## The one-time and hidden costs

The yearly fee is rarely the whole story. Ask about each of these:

| Charge | What to ask |
|---|---|
| Admission fee | Is it one-time? Is any of it refundable? |
| Registration fee | Is it adjusted against fees if you enrol? |
| Security deposit | When and how is it returned? |
| Annual or development charge | Is it charged every year? |
| Meals | Included, or charged monthly? |
| Transport | Per month or per term? Fixed or by distance? |
| Late pickup | Per minute, per hour or per incident? |
| Activities and events | Are there extra charges for trips, costumes or classes? |
| Uniform and books | Bought from the centre, or anywhere? |

Our full [daycare fees explainer](/blog/daycare-fees-explained/) covers each one, including refund terms.

## How to budget for the first year

Work out the true first-year cost for each centre on your shortlist. It's simple:

1. Take the annual fee (or monthly fee × 12).
2. Add every one-time charge: admission, registration, deposit.
3. Add meals, transport and any late-pickup hours you'll realistically need.
4. Add a small buffer for events and supplies.

Then compare totals, not monthly fees. A centre with a lower monthly fee but a large admission fee can cost more in year one.

Remember the second year too. Ask whether fees rise each year and by how much. Ask what you'd pay if you moved from half-day to full-day.

## Fee isn't everything

It's easy to let price lead. Try to keep it as one factor among several. Safety, staff, ratio and your child's happiness matter more over a full year.

Our [complete checklist for choosing a daycare](/blog/how-to-choose-a-daycare/) and the side-by-side scorecard help you weigh fees against everything else. For more on the local picture, see our [guide to daycare in Gurgaon](/blog/daycare-in-gurgaon-guide/).

When Kribble launches, you'll be able to see admission, registration, monthly, quarterly, half-yearly and annual plans side by side for each listed centre.

## Frequently asked questions

### What is the average preschool fee in Gurgaon?

Kiddenz's Gurgaon listings show a median annual fee of about ₹55,400. The range runs from roughly ₹16,000 to ₹2 lakh a year. Your area, the hours you need and what's included will move the number a lot.

### Why are fees in some sectors so much higher?

Rent is likely part of it, since space costs more in high-end sectors. Centres there may also offer longer hours or more facilities. On Kiddenz, Sector 51's median is about ₹1.1 lakh, while Sector 92's is about ₹32,400.

### Is the admission fee refundable?

It depends on the centre, and many admission fees are not. Ask before you pay, and get the answer in writing. Registration fees and security deposits often have different rules, so ask about each.

### Should I pay preschool fees yearly or monthly?

Yearly can be cheaper if there's a discount, but it's harder to leave. Monthly or quarterly gives you flexibility in the first year while you see how your child settles. Check the refund policy either way.
